newsitem.title: UK: IPE says new gas oil rules to protect smaller user.
newsitem.headline: IPE says new gas oil rules to protect smaller user.

text.p: London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) said on Wednesday that tough new rules for its gas oil futures contract were designed to protect small companies using it to hedge risk.
IPE executives told reporters on Wednesday they were prepared to protect smaller users against the type of speculative trading ploy which disrupted European heating oil supplies last winter.

"We have to ensure the gas oil contract meets the needs of users as originally intended - large numbers of end-users using it for hedging purposes," said Richard Ward, the IPE's executive vice-president of business development.
The exchange on Monday voted to introduce new rules aimed at limiting the possibility of the contract being hijacked by overly speculative plays and says it will come down hard on transgressors.

"I give a personal undertaking to take on board the recommendations and we will enforce rules rigorously," said IPE chief executive Lynton Jones. "We have been tightening up enforcement and this will continue," he told reporters on Wednesday.

Jones said the exchange was ready for a short term dip in volume if some of the larger players reduced activity, but that in the longer term the return of natural hedges would help persuade large traders to become fully involved again.
A review by energy consultant Sally Clubley had characterised the IPE as ineffective enforcers susceptible to trader pressure.
"We hope to restore credibility and bring back those in the market who had expressed concern about the contract," Jones said.

Some large players have criticised the imposition by the IPE of new limits on traders retaining large open positions ahead of each month's expiry, claiming the move will reduce traded volumes and hit contract liquidity.
Smaller players who are prone to be buffeted when large squeezes are played out have welcomed the changes.

The new rules, which need to go past the London Clearance House (LCH), Office of Fair Trading (OFT) and the Securities and Investment Board (SIB), are that IPE clients would be fined 100 percent of their entire open position if they exceed 3,500 lots of open interest in the five business days before expirty.

A fine of 50 percent of the contract value will be levied if the open interest exceeds 7,000 lots in the 6-10 days before expiry. The fine falls to 25 percent of the contract value if the open interest exceeds 12,5000 lots in 11-15 days before expiry.
An additional charge will be levied on each excess lot.
Previously there has been no open interest limit which traders say allowed a record 865,100 tonne delivery in November 1996 that led to a stand-off between Cargill and AIC.
"The new measures are preventative rather than a cure," said Ward.
There will be no routine exemptions to the open interest levels, although exceptions may be made in "extreme circumstances" the IPE said in a statement.
Monitoring of open positions on the gas oil contract will be enhanced, said John Mackeoni, executive vice-president of compliance.
"To stop the risk of a disorderly market we will take whatever action is necessary," he said.

A delivery committee will be appointed made up of IPE members and trade representatives which will be able to appoint within 24 hours of a delivery a sub-committee to determine any breach of rules by buyers or sellers.
After expiry the IPE says oil should be in tank by the beginning of the delivery period. In addition random checks will be made to confirm oil is in place.
The IPE said it was not possible to determine exactly when the new regulations are likely to come into force.
"We aim to have them (the new rules) introduced by the winter cycle," said Ward.
